messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver...). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male's profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I've come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

2. Second- while the second set of results above seem reasonable- they're not exactly accurate. Specifically, this network has 13,476 men, 11,524 women, and 17,971 female/male ties. So by my calculation- if we impose the above restrictions (i.e. assume only female/male ties are possible)- the edges coefficient should be -9.064, not -10.457. Such miscalculations occur elsewhere as well- see, for instance, the following model run in statnet compared to an equivalent estimation in Stata (where Stata produces the correct results). Finally, something weird appears to be happening the larger the model gets (and in fact, particularly when the model gets right up against the limit I set in MPLE.max.dyad.types, which I believe here I increased to 1e+7). In the first model, everything seems to be running normally. In the second model, I add an additional set of terms (namely, nodefactor terms related to income); and while the parameter estimates still seem reasonable, all of a sudden the standard errors increase tenfold, almost nothing is significant, and the AIC and BIC skyrocket. (Note, however, that this is not something weird with the income terms- the same thing happens in the third model, when I try religion terms instead of income.) Again, all of this is going on in the territory when the model is about as big as it could possibly get- adding many more terms means it exceeds the max.dyad.types limit- and this seems to be the only time when I run into this particular kind of problem.

Hi Kevin -

I started looking at this, and one quick question to  clarify.  How is your network object "female_views" set up?  I think from reading through your code that it is not bipartite, it has 0s for all the M->M, M->F and F->F ties, and for the attribute "female", 1=female and 0 = male, yes?  Just double-checking that I have the network 100% right before I delve into recreating things.

Steve

On 8/4/2014 3:52 PM, Lewis, Kevin wrote:
Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver...). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male's profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I've come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

Hi Kevin -

I'm still looking into your issues - it seems to be something deep. In 
the meanwhile, I will mention that there is a workaround that seems to 
work just fine.  Try representing your network as an undirected 
bipartite network.  Bipartite makes the M-M and F-F ties into structural 
zeros.  And undirected, because there really is only possible 
relationship of interest for you within each dyad, given your focus on 
F->M ties; this means that the M->F ties are not being modeled.  I 
tested this, and it works fine, giving you the expected log-odds for the 
simple edges only models.  Hopefully, all of the other terms you are 
interested in can be represented in this format, using the various b1... 
and b2... parameters.

This is probably the way I would have gone about it in the first place - 
it seems a bit neater to remove the structural zeros by force in advance 
when possible.  But you're absolutely right that your method should 
still work fine, and doesn't seem to be.

Yours,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Steve,

Thanks for your help, and I really appreciate this suggestion below! You'll have to forgive me- a long time ago I think we had another exchange on this list where, using similar data, I wanted to do something that the bipartite ERGMs couldn't yet handle and so I got stuck in my ways using this alternative approach; but it's great to know this alternative option is available.

Please know, then, that the solution to the problem I documented isn't urgent- but I'm still curious to hear what you find!

Thanks again and best wishes,
Kevin

From: statnet_help [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman13.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Steven Goodreau
Sent: Tuesday, August 05, 2014 5:06 PM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] MPLE with offset terms

Hi Kevin -

I'm still looking into your issues - it seems to be something deep.  In the meanwhile, I will mention that there is a workaround that seems to work just fine.  Try representing your network as an undirected bipartite network.  Bipartite makes the M-M and F-F ties into structural zeros.  And undirected, because there really is only possible relationship of interest for you within each dyad, given your focus on F->M ties; this means that the M->F ties are not being modeled.  I tested this, and it works fine, giving you the expected log-odds for the simple edges only models.  Hopefully, all of the other terms you are interested in can be represented in this format, using the various b1... and b2... parameters.

This is probably the way I would have gone about it in the first place - it seems a bit neater to remove the structural zeros by force in advance when possible.  But you're absolutely right that your method should still work fine, and doesn't seem to be.

Yours,
Steve

Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver...). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male's profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I've come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

On 8/4/2014 3:52 PM, Lewis, Kevin wrote:
Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver?). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male?s profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I?ve come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jesse,

maybe I am wrong, but as far as I know, the nacf-function in sna only 
calculates the coefficient, not its standard error nor the test result 
for departure from randomness. Syntax:

    nacf(network,attribute,type='moran',neighborhood.type='out')[2]

Index [2] is needed for extracting the direct (at geodesic outgoing 
distance 1) neighbours' autocorrelation (index [1] stands for 
autocorrelation at distance zero, i.e., self-correlation=value one; 
higher indices stand for correlations larger geodesic outgoing distances).

For the testing, I guess you could use the sna-function cugtest, but 
that might give a different type of null hypothesis tested than what 
Moran envisioned.

There also is a pre-programmed Moran's I in the package 'ape' (called 
Moran.I) which does give the st.error and significance test according to 
Moran. Funny thing is, last time I tried, the Moran calculations by 
UCINET, sna and ape tended to give slightly different results, for 
reasons I didn't understand at the time - probably related to 
directedness of the network or missing data entries. I ended up 
programming my own, to be sure what happens.

Best,
Christian

messages.body_plain:
Nodefactor is a term that will capture only Marginal effects by factor 
level

* e.g., heterogeneity in mean degree by factor level

nodematch is different -- it captures homophily effects.

* e.g., heterogeneity in the probability of a tie as a function of 
matching nodal attributes (homophily)

and in general, if you want to test for homophily effects, you should 
have both nodefactor and nodematch terms in your model.

in addition, if you think there are differential rates of homophily by 
node factor level, you can test for this using nodematch("attr", diff=T). 
this again is a mode specification.

* it allow for different levels of homophily by nodefactor level.

these are three separate specifications; the idea is to test which one 
fits the data best.

hth,
mm

can generalize this into a splitNetworks function which would give you a

splitNetworks<-function(net,attrname){
   # find the unique values
   vals<-get.edge.attribute(net,attrname)
   uniqueVals<-unique(vals)
   nets<-list()
   # for each value of attrname, create a network
   # containing only edges that have that value
   for (val in uniqueVals){
     subNet<-net
     delete.edges(subNet,eid=which(vals!=val))
     nets<-c(nets,list(subNet))
   }
   # name the elements of the list according to values
   names(nets)<-uniqueVals
   return(nets)
}

The network() conversion function is expecting that your ids are 
integers from 1 to the size of the network. Since your ids are very big, 
it creates a very big network.  However, if you trick it into seeing the 
ids as labels, it will probably do what you want.  You can do this by 
converting the unitid and punit ids into characters instead of numeric 
values

character columns

 > net<-network(rawData[,1:2])

 > set.edge.attribute(net,'distance',rawData[,3])
 > net
  Network attributes:
   vertices = 15
   directed = TRUE
   hyper = FALSE
   loops = FALSE
   multiple = FALSE
   bipartite = FALSE
   total edges= 15
     missing edges= 0
     non-missing edges= 15

  Vertex attribute names:
     vertex.names

     distance

  [1] "100636" "100654" "100663" "100690" "100706" "100724" "100733" 
"100751" "100760" "100812" "100830" "100858"
[13] "100937" "101028" "101073"


The challenge of course is that you can't use your big ids directly in 
queries, you have to match them back to your vertex.names attribute like

 > get.edgeIDs(net,v=match("100654",network.vertex.names(net)),
             alter=match("100636",network.vertex.names(net)))
[1] 2



If you need to do a bunch of work tracking these external ids, you may 
want to use the 'persistent id' functionality in the networkDynamic package

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] QAP for a single regression independent variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Let me summarize your situation: You've got (a) an outcome variable on 
the nodes, (b) a network matrix that shows the dependencies between your 
units of observation, (c) an independent variable which is derived from 
this matrix, and (d) a bunch of other independent variables at the node 
level. Correct?

In that case, it is not the variable in (c) which introduces the bias 
into the model. It is rather the matrix in (b) which causes your trouble 
because your observations are not independent. (c) is rather a partial 
remedy for the problem because you are modeling parts of the 
dependencies as part of the data-generating process.

It would be ideal if you could also incorporate other types of 
dependencies which explain your outcome variable in order to reduce the 
bias, which may be framed as a special kind of omitted variable bias.

For example, it may be the average outcome of actor i's contacts j that 
influences i's outcome. Or it may be i's total exposure to the sum of 
all of i's contacts j's outcomes. Or maybe i's outcome is affected by 
the friends k of his friends j (i.e., indirect friends). Or maybe i 
compares his or her potential outcome to that of other nodes j which are 
connected to the same other nodes k, which is essentially structural 
similarity. Or maybe i's cliques' outcomes influence i's outcomes (to a 
greater extent than bilateral influence). Or perhaps isolates have 
different outcomes than connected nodes etc.

The basic version of this is called the linear network autocorrelation 
model, and it was implemented in the lnam function in the sna package. 
But this function can only control for the first of the dependencies 
outlined above. A more comprehensive solution would be the tnam function 
("temporal network autocorrelation model") in the xergm package. It 
includes all of the above-mentioned dependencies and some others for any 
kind of dependent variable (not just a linear model) and possibly 
including random effects and possibly modeling multiple time steps 
(which would enable you to assess diffusion of behavior over time).

The caveat is that this kind of model does not tell you which 
dependencies you have to model. This is part of the modeling process, 
just like the way you model dependencies in an ERGM by adding some more 
model terms and checking if this improves the model fit. But you can 
never know if you have captured all of the dependencies (but I guess you 
have to live with this in the ERGM world, too).

It should be obvious now that a QAP approach does not really help you 
out because it is not your independent variable that is causing the bias 
but rather your network dependencies and the omitted variable bias 
resulting from the unmodeled dependencies.

So my answers to your three questions would be:

1. It affects all parameters, but the reason is not the independent 
variable.

2. I think this would not work because the dependent variable would 
still be contaminated by autocorrelation because your observations are 
nested in the network.

3. I don't know, but I think the question got obsolete now.

Does anybody have a better solution for this kind of problem? I'd be 
curious to hear about it because I am relatively new to the world of 
autocorrelation models; I just implemented the tnam stuff this month.

Best,
Philip

Dear Steve (and Kirk and Li),

Thank you so much for your help!!! I only hope I can continue doing things that are sufficiently odd that I stumble across bugs that otherwise escaped detection :).

Best wishes,
Kevin

From: statnet_help [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman13.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Steven Goodreau
Sent: Thursday, August 28, 2014 9:23 AM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] MPLE with offset terms

Hello Kevin--

It turns out that you did indeed uncover a bug.  And it's something that only arose when one had a dyadic independent model and multiple offset terms - a sufficiently unique experience that we hadn't caught it before, but our students Kirk and Li were able to track it down.  It will be fixed in the next release, which we anticipate should be in the next month or so.

Thanks again for bringing this up - we rely on folks doing this to make the software better for everyone.

Yours,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Dear Achim,

On Tue, 2014-08-26 at 08:07 +1000, Achim Edelmann, Ph.D. wrote:
> Dear Statnet group, 
> 
> this is a question about the STERGM.  I would like to know if and how
> it is possible to include stable and, eventually, even (externally)
> changing dyad covariates.  Say, for example, I would like to model the
> formation/dissolution of relationships among a small group of
> neighbors over several waves.  How could I include a term for whether
> people had known each other before the first wave?  

You can do it by using an edgecov term. Generally, almost all ergm terms
still work.

> And, ideally, how
> could I include a term for the (exogenously) changing distances
> between their work places?  Can STERGM handle any of this and, if so,
> how to best feed the model with the stable/changing matrices in R?

For setting edge covariates, I would suggest taking a look at ergm
tutorials. You will need to construct a network with the attributes and
covariates you are looking for, then give the stergm() call a list of
the networks in the series.

                                  I hope this helps,
                                  Pavel
